text:
Teixeira c. Pantazopoulos

2024 QCCQ 1317

COURT OF QUÉBEC

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUÉBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTRÉAL

“Civil
Division”

No:

500-22-273079-221

DATE:

April 5, 2024

______________________________________________________________________

PRESIDED BY THE HONORABLE MÉLANIE
DUGRÉ, J.C.Q.

______________________________________________________________________

ARMENIA TEIXEIRA

Plaintiff

v.

DIMITRA PANTAZOPOULOS

Defendant

and

GOLDWATER DUBÉ INC.

and

BANQUE TD CANADA TRUST &
GESTION DU PATRIMOINE

Impleaded Parties

__________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

Dimitra Pantazopoulos retained the services of Me
Armenia Teixeira to represent her in legal matters of a family nature.

[
2
]

A dispute arose regarding the legal fees charged
by Me Teixeira, which led to arbitration decisions dated May 22 and June 15,
2022, condemning Ms. Pantazopoulos to pay $78,186.22 in legal fees to Me
Teixeira.
[1]

[
3
]

Me Teixeira sought the homologation of the
arbitration decision, which was granted by Justice Enrico Forlini on October
18, 2022.

[
4
]

Among other seizure measures taken to execute
the judgment, Me Teixeira seized Ms. Pantazopoulos’ vehicle, as well as bank and
TFSA accounts.
[2]

[
5
]

Ms. Pantazopoulos is opposing the seizure of
these three items and asking for their release.

[
6
]

Ms. Pantazopoulos acknowledges that she has
remained the guardian of the vehicle since the October 18, 2022 seizure and has
continued to use it.

[
7
]

Ms. Pantazopoulos contends that she cannot remit
the vehicle because she needs it to attend medical appointments, and that she
cannot pay bills due to the seizure on the bank account. She adds that Me
Teixeira should obtain payment from a seizure before judgment performed in
October 2022 on the trust account of a notary, for an amount of $210,907.37.

ISSUES

[
8
]

a)   Is Ms. Pantazopoulos’ vehicle exempt from
seizure?

b)

Is the seizure on Ms. Pantazopoulos’ bank and
TFSA accounts valid?

c)

Should Me Teixeira obtain payment exclusively
from the seizure before judgment performed on the notary’s trust account?

ANALYSIS
AND DECISION

a)

Is Ms. Pantazopoulos’ vehicle exempt from
seizure
?

[
9
]

The law
provides that the execution of a judgment may be forced if the debtor refuses
to comply voluntarily and the judgment has become final, which is the case here.
[3]

[
10
]

Furthermore, the property of a debtor
constitutes the security for their creditors.
[4]
A creditor who holds an enforceable judgment against a person can
seize property belonging to that person.

[
11
]

The law states
that any person under a personal obligation charges, for its performance, all
his property, movable and immovable, present, and future, except property which
is exempt from seizure.
[5]

[
12
]

The seizable nature of a property is the rule,
and exemption from seizure is the exception. Any exemption from seizure must
rely on a clear and precise legal provision, and the person seeking exemption
from seizure has the burden of proof.
[6]

[
13
]

Insofar as motor vehicles are concerned, the law
states that a passenger motor vehicle cannot be seized if it is necessary to
meet the basic needs of the debtor and the debtor’s dependants, or to ensure
that they receive the care required by their state of health.

[
14
]

However, the law also specifies that a motor
vehicle may be seized if the debtor can meet essential travel needs by using
public transit or another available vehicle.
[7]

[
15
]

Ms. Pantazopoulos contends that she will need
her vehicle to take care of her children once she regains their custody.

[
16
]

At the present time, Ms. Pantazopoulos does not
have custody of her children, and the Court cannot rely on the hypothesis that
this situation may eventually change in assessing whether the seizure of the
vehicle is valid.

[
17
]

Furthermore, Ms. Pantazopoulos alleges that she
needs the vehicle to attend medical appointments in the context where she
suffers from various health problems.

[
18
]

Recent caselaw
[8]

confirmed that it is insufficient for a debtor to show that it would be useful
or advantageous to have their vehicle to attend medical appointments.
Convincing evidence must be offered that the vehicle is necessary, unavoidable,
and essential for the debtor to receive the care required by their health
condition.

[
19
]

Courts also insist that utility of a vehicle
should not be confused with its necessity.
[9]

[
20
]

To support her allegation that she needs her
vehicle for medical reasons, Ms. Pantazopoulos submits six medical notes
or letters from the Jewish General Hospital. Most of them simply confirm existing
diagnosis and treatment plans.
[10]

[
21
]

Two of those documents, one dated December 11, 2023,
and the other, February 12, 2024, only state that Ms. Pantazopoulos needs
her vehicle to attend medical appointments.

[
22
]

The letters are however silent as to why Ms. Pantazopoulos’
medical condition would render the use of a vehicle necessary and why she could
not use other transportation means.

[
23
]

Ms. Pantazopoulos argues that she must avoid
being in public because she suffers from an autoimmune disease, which makes her
vulnerable to viruses. The only evidence supporting this allegation is a June
2020 note, which was drafted when the Covid-19 pandemic was raging. None of the
most recent medical notes recommend that Ms. Pantazopoulos minimizes
contact outside her home due to a medical condition.

[
24
]

The Court also notes that Ms. Pantazopoulos has
been living at her parents’ house in Brossard for quite some time and that
public transportation from Brossard to the Jewish General Hospital is
easily accessible.

[
25
]

The Court finds that the evidence offered does
not demonstrate that Ms. Pantazopoulos needs her vehicle to obtain the
care required by her health condition.

[
26
]

Consequently, the Court concludes that Ms.
Pantazopoulos’ vehicle is not exempt from seizure.

b)

Is the seizure on Ms. Pantazopoulos’ bank
and TFSA accounts valid
?

[
27
]

On January 23, 2023, TD Canada Trust in Pointe-Claire
provided a positive statement to a notice of execution and confirmed that Ms.
Pantozopoulos held a bank account with a balance of $195.07 and a TFSA account
with a balance of $179.75.

[
28
]

Ms. Pantazopoulos contends that she is prevented
from paying her creditors due to the seizure of her bank account and that she
is being harassed by collection measures.

[
29
]

The fact that creditors are sending collection
letters to Ms. Pantazopoulos is unrelated to the seizure of her bank account.
Should Ms. Pantazopoulos be determined to pay her creditors, she certainly has
other ways to make such payments.

[
30
]

Access to these specific accounts, while she has
bank accounts in other financial institutions, is certainly not a condition for
Ms. Pantazopoulos to pay her creditors.

[
31
]

The arguments brought forward by Ms.
Pantozopoulos are insufficient to put aside the principle that seizability is
the rule, and exemption from seizure is the exception.

[
32
]

The Court therefore concludes that the seizure
on Ms. Pantazopoulos’ bank and TFSA accounts is valid.

c)

Should Me Teixeira obtain payment
exclusively from the seizure before judgment performed on the notary’s trust
account?

[
33
]

Prior to Justice Forlini’s judgment of October
18, 2022, Me Teixeira obtained the Court’s authorization to proceed with a
seizure before judgment, and on October 13, 2022, Me Josée Deschamps,
notary, confirmed that her trust account contained $210,907.37 belonging to Ms.
Pantazopoulos further to the sale of the family residence.
[11]

[
34
]

However, Me Deschamps specified that the money
could not be released because, prior to receiving Me Teixeira’s notice of
execution, another law firm, Goldwater Dubé, served her with seizure
proceedings on October 4, 2022. This seizure before judgment is related to file
500-17-106548-194 before the Superior Court in which Goldwater Dubé, which also
represented Ms. Pantozopoulos’ interests in previous litigation matters, is
seeking payment of its legal fees.
[12]

[
35
]

Ms. Pantazopoulos filed an opposition to
Goldwater Dubé’s seizure before judgment, and this issue has been referred to
the judge who will hear the merit of the case on September 10, 2024.

[
36
]

In the meantime, Me Teixeira and Goldwater Dubé
reached an agreement regarding the distribution between them of the amount
seized in the notary’s trust account, should the Superior Court declare the
seizure to be valid. This agreement provides that Me Teixeira will receive
$33,267.06 and the balance will go to Goldwater Dubé.

[
37
]

As a result, a portion of Ms. Pantozopoulos’
debt will nonetheless remain unpaid, which explains why Me Teixeira proceeded
to the seizure after judgment of the vehicle and bank accounts, which Ms.
Pantazopoulos is opposing.

[
38
]

At the hearing, Ms. Pantazopoulos states that
she wants to withdraw her contestation of Goldwater Dubé’s seizure before
judgment on the notary’s trust account. She therefore asks that Me Teixeira
executes the October 18, 2022 judgment on this seizure.

[
39
]

This argument does not constitute a reason,
among those listed under article 735 C.C.P., that can be invoked to
cancel a seizure after judgment.

[
40
]

Furthermore, Ms. Pantazopoulos is asking this
Court to rule on the distribution of the amount seized in the notary’s trust
account by ordering Me Teixeira to obtain full payment of her claim from the
trust account, and cancelling seizure of the vehicle and accounts.

[
41
]

However, it is not the Court’s role to rule on
the distribution of the seized property among the various creditors.

[
42
]

Indeed,
the law states that
acts necessary for the purpose of executing a
judgment are performed by a court bailiff who may, while executing a judgment,
ask the court for any instruction he needs to act.
[13]

[
43
]

This means that the creditor must provide his
instructions to the bailiff
[14]

who is then responsible for distributing the proceeds of the sale or the sums
seized to the creditors.
[15]

[
44
]

The law is therefore clear that the process of
forced execution and distribution of the sums seized fall under the bailiff’s
responsibility.

[
45
]

As a result, the Court’s role is limited to
determining whether there exists a valid reason to oppose the seizure, which
would justify its cancellation.

[
46
]

As for the agreement between Goldwater Dubé and
Me Teixeira regarding the distribution of the amount seized in the notary’s
trust account, it only binds the contracting party.
[16]

[
47
]

Moreover, the consequence of this agreement will
only become relevant at the time the bailiff with prepare the collocation
scheme and distribute the sums seized further to Goldwater Dubé’s seizure, a
matter which is before the Superior Court.

[
48
]

In the context of her opposition to Me
Teixeira’s seizure after judgment, Ms. Pantazopoulos had the burden to
first prove that she needed the vehicle to receive the
care required by her state of health.

[
49
]

She also had to prove that the seizure of the
bank and TFRA accounts was invalid.

[
50
]

Ms. Pantazopoulos did not meet her burden of
proof on either issue. Her opposition to the seizure is therefore dismissed.

FOR
THESE REASONS, THE COURT:

DISMISSES
Dimitra Pantazopoulos’
Demande en
opposition à la saisie
and
Demande en révision
de la décision de l’huissier
;

THE WHOLE,
with costs.
